answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. a Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: CLI group: az cosmosdb (core Azure CLI). Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group MyRG --locations regionName=eastus --kind MongoDB. (The az cosmosdb group is in the core CLI, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM resource: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (use the appropriate apiVersion e.g. '2021-04-15' or newer). Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (in the azurerm provider).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Mongo-compatible URI for Azure DocumentDB / Cosmos DB (Mongo API) looks like: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Use TLS/SSL=true (or tls=true), host usually ends with .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and TLS port 10255. (SRV syntax is not generally used for Cosmos Mongo API historically.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos throughput (RUs): provisioned RU/s (manual or autoscale) or serverless in supported regions. It is RU-based rather than direct vCore-based pricing for the Mongo-compatible API (management plane uses Azure resource billing).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane authentication for Mongo API is username/password (SCRAM: SCRAM-SHA-1 / SCRAM-SHA-256) using the account database credentials or user accounts created in the database. Management operations use Azure AD; the Mongo data API typically does not accept Microsoft Entra ID OAuth tokens for regular driver connections — drivers should authenticate with the Mongo credentials in the connection string. (Use Azure AD for management/ARM operations only.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the target language (e.g., mongodb npm package for Node.js). There is no separate data-plane, service-specific MongoDB client SDK — the Azure SDKs are for management. For Node.js: npm install mongodb and connect with MongoClient to the provided connection string.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: I expect vector index support (as described in the sample) to include DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. The exact create-index syntax is product-specific; a plausible command in the managed Mongo-compatible surface would be a collection-level index API similar to: db.content_pieces.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'idx_embedding_hnsw', algorithm: 'HNSW', M: 16, efConstruction: 200, distance: 'cosine' }). However, this is a best-guess — the real service may expose a JSON-style index creation API or an admin command rather than a pure createIndex() option.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Basic text search can be done with MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })). For advanced full-text/hybrid (text + vector) search on Azure, you typically integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or a service-specific vector-search index feature if the managed cluster provides one; otherwise combine text indexes and vector indexes at the application/query layer.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Typical managed Azure Mongo-compatible offerings advertise compatibility with specific MongoDB server wire versions (recent offerings claim compatibility with MongoDB 6.0 or 7.0 wire protocol). Common mismatches vs upstream MongoDB historically include: incomplete support for server-side JavaScript ($where), some aggregation stages or pipeline optimizations, cross-shard multi-document transactions or some transaction semantics, and occasionally limited change-stream/oplog access. (For this environment the sample states MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol support.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is a Cosmos DB emulator for some APIs, but for Mongo-compatible development it's safest to run a local MongoDB Docker image. Example: docker run -d -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7.0. Use port 27017 for local Mongo. (Don't store the live cluster connection string in code; use env var.)

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams require oplog access / a replica-set topology and a Mongo server version that supports change streams (>= 3.6). On managed clusters change streams are available when the service exposes the oplog (replica set) — sometimes you need to enable or request oplog access or use a replica-set connection string. Expect to have to ensure the account exposes a proper replica-set endpoint; the exact enablement may be provider-specific.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (documentdb profile) for data-plane inspection and tools targeted at this managed Mongo-compatible service. The generic Azure MCP server covers resource management, but data-plane DB inspection (collections, indexes, query plans) is provided by the documentdb MCP server and its 'default' connection profile in the sample environment.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally used the name DocumentDB for the predecessor to Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB evolved from DocumentDB and now exposes multiple APIs (Core/SQL, MongoDB API, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). The 'DocumentDB' name historically referred to Microsoft's proprietary document database; it is not the same as any independent open-source 'DocumentDB' project. When people say 'DocumentDB' today they often mean Azure's document database lineage (Cosmos DB).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API the underlying engine is the provider's implementation that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol (in Azure's case the Cosmos DB engine implementing Mongo compatibility, or a managed MongoDB engine in a dedicated managed Mongo service). From application code you should use standard MongoDB drivers and expect mostly-compatible behavior, but some server features, limits and query planner behaviors can differ — test critical queries and functionality against the managed cluster.

answers.question: What database name should this sample use for everything it creates?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_14 for all sample-created collections and queries.

answers.question: How should the sample read the cluster connection at runtime and what driver options should it pass?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI. In Node.js use the mongodb driver: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, useUnifiedTopology: true }); then await client.connect(). (Do not write the URI to files or logs.)

answers.question: Which collections and indexes will the sample create (names and the vector index requirement)?
answers.answer: Collections to create: customers, segments, interactions, content_pieces, embeddings. The sample needs a vector index on content_pieces.embedding (vector) capable of nearest-neighbour search; a plausible create command (service-specific) is: db.content_pieces.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'idx_embedding_hnsw', algorithm: 'HNSW', M: 16, efConstruction: 200, distance: 'cosine' }). (Use the cluster's index API if createIndex() does not support these options.)

answers.question: Which client library and Node.js packages will the sample use to implement the LlamaIndex agent and DB access?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb Node.js driver (npm install mongodb@^5). For the LlamaIndex/agent parts use the Node LlamaIndex package or the recommended Node.js LLM integration libs (install per the latest LlamaIndex Node instructions). Connect to the DB with MongoClient and fetch documents for the agent memory and retrieval components.

answers.question: Which MCP command will the sample use to verify collections and indexes using the documentdb MCP server profile 'default'?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server commands, for example: mcp documentdb inspect collection sample_customer_360_14.content_pieces --profile default (to list indexes and query plan). If a different subcommand is required, use the documentdb server's inspect/index or explain commands against the same connection profile 'default'.
